exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Domain Where a Partial Derivative Exists

question.text: Given that $f(x,y)=\dfrac{\sqrt{x + y}}y,$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ exists.
question.explanation:
First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined only when

\begin{align*} x + y &\geq 0 \quad \text{and} \quad y \ne 0. \end{align*}

So, the domain of $f$ is \[ D_f = \{(x,y) \, : \, y \ne 0 \:\text{and}\: x+y \geq 0 \}. \]

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial} {\partial y}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{x + y}}y\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{y \cdot \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x + y}} - \sqrt{x + y}}{y^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{y - 2x - 2y}{2y^2\sqrt{x + y}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-2x-y}{2y^2\sqrt{x + y}} \end{align*}

The function $f_y(x,y)$ is defined only for

\begin{align*} y \ne 0 \quad \text{and} \quad x + y > 0. \end{align*}

So, the domain of $f_y$ is

\[ D_{f_y} = \big\{ (x,y) \,:\, y \ne 0 \:\text{and}\: x+y > 0 \big\}. \]

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

\begin{align*} D_f \cap D_{f_y} &= \{(x,y) \, : \, y \ne 0 \:\text{and}\: x+y \geq 0 \} \cap \big\{ (x,y) \,:\, y \ne 0 \:\text{and}\: x+y > 0\big\} \\[3pt] &=\big\{ (x,y) \,:\, y \ne 0 \:\text{and}\: x+y > 0\big\}. \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\dfrac{x}{y+z},$ find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ exists.
question.explanation:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)$ is defined only when $y+z \ne 0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is \[ D_f = \big\{(x,y,z) \, : \, y+z \ne 0 \big\}. \]

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} f_y(x,y,z) &= \dfrac {\partial} {\partial y}\left(\dfrac{x}{y+z}\right)\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{x}{(y+z)^2} \end{align}

The function $f_y(x,y,z)$ is defined only for

\begin{align*} (y+z)^2 & \ne 0 \\[3pt] y+z & \ne 0. \end{align*}

So, the domain of $f_y$ is

\[ D_{f_y} = \big\{ (x,y,z) \,:\, y+z \ne 0 \big\}. \]

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

\begin{align*} D_f \cap D_{f_y} &= \big\{ (x,y,z) \,:\, y+z \ne 0 \big\} \cap \big\{ (x,y,z) \,:\, y+z \ne 0 \big\} \\[3pt] &=\big\{ (x,y,z) \,:\, y+z \ne 0 \big\}. \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $f(x,y)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y - x^2}},$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ exists.
question.explanation:
First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined only when

\begin{align*} y - x^2 &> 0 \\[3pt] y &> x^2. \end{align*}

So, the domain of $f$ is \[ D_f = \big\{(x,y) \, : \, y > x^2 \big\}. \]

Now, we compute the partial derivative of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} f_x(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial} {\partial x}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y - x^2}}\right)\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{-2x}{2(y - x^2)^{3/2}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x}{(y - x^2)^{3/2}} \end{align}

The function $f_x(x,y)$ is defined only for \begin{align*} y - x^2 &> 0 \\[3pt] y &> x^2. \end{align*}

So, the domain of $f_x$ is

\[ D_{f_x} = \big\{(x,y) \, : \, y > x^2 \big\}. \]

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ exists on the set \begin{align*} D_f \cap D_{f_x} &= \big\{(x,y) \, : \, y > x^2 \big\} \cap \big\{(x,y) \, : \, y > x^2 \big\}\\[3pt] &=\big\{(x,y) \, : \, y > x^2 \big\}. \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $f(x,y)=x\ln (xy),$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ exists.
question.explanation:
First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined when $xy \gt 0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is \[ D_f = \{(x,y) \, : \, xy \gt 0 \}. \]

Now, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial} {\partial y}\left(x\ln (xy)\right) \\[5pt] &= x \cdot \dfrac{x}{xy} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac xy \end{align*}

The function $f_y(x,y)$ is defined only for \begin{align*} y \ne 0 \end{align*}

So, the domain of $f_y$ is

\[ D_{f_y} = \big\{ (x,y) \,:\, y \ne 0 \big\}. \]

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

\begin{align*} D_f \cap D_{f_y} &= \big\{ (x,y) \,:\, xy \gt 0 \big\} \cap \big\{ (x,y) \,:\, y \ne 0\big\} \\[3pt] &= \big\{ (x,y) \,:\, xy \gt 0 \big\}. \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $f(x,y)=\arcsin\left(xy \right),$ find the set of values $(x,y)$ on which $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ exists.
question.explanation:
First, notice that $f(x,y)$ is defined when $-1 \leq xy \leq 1.$ So, the domain of $f$ is \[ D_f = \{(x,y) \, : \, -1 \leq xy \leq 1 \}. \]

Now, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)$ with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_y(x,y) &= \dfrac {\partial} {\partial y}\left(\arcsin \left(xy\right)\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (xy)^2}} \cdot x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2y^2}} \end{align*}

The function $f_y(x,y)$ is defined only for \begin{align*} 1 - x^2y^2 &\gt 0\\[3pt] x^2y^2 & \lt 1 \\[3pt] -1 \lt xy &\lt 1. \end{align*}

So, the domain of $f_y$ is

\[ D_{f_y} = \big\{ (x,y) \,:\, -1 < xy < 1 \big\}. \]

Finally, we conclude that the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ exists on the set

\begin{align*} D_f \cap D_{f_y} &= \big\{ (x,y) \,:\, -1 \leq xy \leq 1 \big\} \cap \big\{ (x,y) \,:\, -1 < xy < 1 \big\} \\[3pt] &= \big\{ (x,y) \,:\, -1 < xy < 1 \big\}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist

question.text: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\arctan(x+y+z)$ and \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} = \dfrac{1}{1+(x+y+z)^2}, \] find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
question.explanation:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\arctan(x+y+z)$ is defined for any $x$, $y$, and $z.$ So, the domain of $f$ is \[ D_f = \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x,y,z \in (-\infty,\infty) \}. \]

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

  • The function $f_x=\dfrac{1}{1+(x+y+z)^2}$ is defined for any $x$, $y$, and $z.$ So, the domain of $f_x$ is \[ D_{f_x} = \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x,y,z \in (-\infty,\infty) \}. \]

  • Similarly, the domains of $f_y$ and $f_z$ are \[ D_{f_y} = D_{f_z} = \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x,y,z \in (-\infty,\infty) \}. \]

Therefore, we conclude that the partial derivatives of $f$ exist on the set

\begin{align*} D_f \cap D_{f_x} \cap D_{f_y} \cap D_{f_z} &= D_f \cap D_{f_x} \\[3pt] &= \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x,y,z \in (-\infty,\infty) \} \cap \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x,y,z \in (-\infty,\infty) \} \\[3pt] &= \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x,y,z \in (-\infty,\infty) \}. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist

question.text: Given that $h(x,y,z)=\ln\left(\dfrac{xz}{y^2}\right)$ and \[ \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial x} =\dfrac{1}{x}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial y} =-\dfrac{2}{y}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial z} =\dfrac{1}{z}, \] find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $h$ exist.
question.explanation:
First, notice that $h(x,y,z)=\ln\left(\dfrac{xz}{y^2}\right)$ is defined only when $xz > 0$ and $y \neq 0.$ So, the domain of $h$ is \[ D_h = \{(x,y,z) \, : \, xz > 0 \:\text{and}\: y \neq 0 \}. \]

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

  • The function $h_x =\dfrac{1}{x}$ is defined only when $x \neq 0.$ So, the domain of $h_x$ is \[ D_{h_x} = \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x \neq 0 \}. \]

  • The function $h_y =-\dfrac{2}{y}$ is defined only when $y \neq 0.$ So, the domain of $h_y$ is \[ D_{h_y} = \{(x,y,z) \, : \, y \neq 0 \}. \]

  • The function $h_z =\dfrac{1}{z}$ is defined only when $z \neq 0.$ So, the domain of $h_z$ is \[ D_{h_z} = \{(x,y,z) \, : \, z \neq 0 \}. \]

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $h$ exist on the set

\begin{align*} D_h \cap D_{h_x} \cap D_{h_y} \cap D_{h_z} &= \{(x,y,z) \, : \, xz > 0 \:\text{and}\: y \neq 0 \} \cap \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x \neq 0 \}\\[5pt] & \quad \, \, \, \, \cap \, \{(x,y,z) \, : \, y \neq 0 \} \cap \{(x,y,z) \, : \, z \neq 0 \} \\[5pt] &= \{(x,y, z) \, : \, xz > 0 \:\text{and}\: y \neq 0 \}. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist

question.text: Given that $f(x,y,z)=\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{1 + y -x^2}}$ and \[ \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} =\dfrac{xz}{\sqrt{(1+y-x^2)^3}}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} =-\dfrac{z}{2\sqrt{(1+y-x^2)^3}}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} =\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + y -x^2}}, \] find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
question.explanation:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\dfrac{z}{\sqrt{1 + y -x^2}}$ is defined only when $1 + y -x^2 > 0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is \[ D_f = \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x^2 < y + 1 \}. \]

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

  • The function $f_x =\dfrac{xz}{\sqrt{(1+y-x^2)^3}}$ is defined only when $1+y-x^2 > 0.$ So, the domain of $f_x$ is \[ D_{f_x} = \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x^2 < y + 1 \}. \]

  • Similarly, the domain of $f_y$ and $f_z$ are the same \[ D_{f_y} = D_{f_z} = \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x^2 < y + 1 \}. \]

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

\begin{align*} D_f \cap D_{f_x} \cap D_{f_y} \cap D_{f_z} &= D_f \cap D_{f_x} \\[3pt] &= \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x^2 < y + 1 \} \cap \{(x,y,z) \, : \, x^2 < y + 1 \} \\[3pt] &= \{(x,y, z) \, : \, x^2 < y + 1 \}. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist

question.text: Given that $g(x,y)= x\ln(x^2+y^2)$ and \[ \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} = \dfrac{2x^2}{x^2+y^2} + \ln(x^2+y^2), \qquad \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} = \dfrac{2xy}{x^2+y^2}, \] find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist.
question.explanation:
First, notice that $g(x,y) = x\ln(x^2+y^2)$ is defined only when $x^2+y^2>0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is \[ D_g = \{(x,y) \, : \, x^2+y^2 > 0 \}. \]

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

  • The function $g_x(x,y) = \dfrac{2x^2}{x^2+y^2} + \ln(x^2+y^2)$ is defined only when $x^2+y^2 > 0.$ So, the domain of $g_x$ is \[ D_{g_x} = \{(x,y) \, : \, x^2+y^2 > 0 \}. \]

  • The function $g_y(x,y) = \dfrac{2xy}{x^2+y^2}$ is defined only when $x^2+y^2 \neq 0.$ So, the domain of $g_y$ is \[ D_{g_y} = \{(x,y) \, : \, x^2+y^2 \neq 0 \}. \]

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

\begin{align*} D_g \cap D_{g_x} \cap D_{g_y} &= \{(x,y) \, : \, x^2+y^2 > 0 \} \cap \{(x,y) \, : \, x^2+y^2 > 0 \} \cap \{(x,y) \, : \, x^2+y^2 \neq 0 \} \\[3pt] &= \{(x,y) \, : \, x^2+y^2 > 0 \}. \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist

question.text: Given that $g(x,y)= \sqrt{x}\,e^{x/y}$ and \[ \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} = \dfrac{(2x+y)e^{x/y}}{2y\sqrt{x}}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{x^3}\,e^{x/y}}{y^2}, \] find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist.
question.explanation:
First, notice that $g(x,y) = \sqrt{x}\,e^{x/y}$ is defined only when $x \geq 0$ and $y \neq 0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is \[ D_g = \{(x,y) \, : \, x \geq 0, y \neq 0 \}. \]

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

  • The function $g_x(x,y) = \dfrac{(2x+y)e^{x/y}}{2y\sqrt{x}}$ is defined only when $x > 0$ and $y \neq 0.$ So, the domain of $g_x$ is \[ D_{g_x} = \{(x,y) \, : \, x > 0, y \neq 0 \}. \]

  • The function $g_y(x,y) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{x^3}e^{x/y}}{y^2}$ is defined only when $x \geq 0$ and $y \neq 0.$ So, the domain of $g_x$ is \[ D_{g_y} = \{(x,y) \, : \, x \geq 0, y \neq 0 \}. \]

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

\begin{align*} D_g \cap D_{g_x} \cap D_{g_y} &= \{(x,y) \, : \, x \geq 0, y \neq 0 \} \cap \{(x,y) \, : \, x > 0, y \neq 0 \} \cap \{(x,y) \, : \, x \geq 0, y \neq 0 \} \\[3pt] &= \{(x,y) \, : \, x > 0, y \neq 0 \}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying Points Where Partial Derivatives Exist

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\ln({xy(z-1)})?$

  1. The partial derivative with respect to $z$ is defined at $(3,2,1)$
  2. $f_y(1,1,2)$ is defined
  3. $f_x(1,2,3)$ is defined
question.explanation:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot y(z-1)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{x} \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = \dfrac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot x(z-1)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{y} \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z} & =\dfrac{1}{xy(z-1)}\cdot xy\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{z-1} \end{align*}

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

  • Statement I is false. If we substitute $(3,2,1)$ into $f$, we get \[ f(3,2,1) = \ln(3\cdot2\cdot(1-1)) = \ln(0), \] which is undefined.

  • Statement II is true. If we substitute $(1,1,2)$ into $f$, we get \[ f(1,1,2) = \ln(1\cdot1\cdot(2-1)) = \ln(1)=0, \] and $f_y$ is also defined at $(1,1,2)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} f_y(1,1,2) &=\dfrac 11 = 1. \end{align*}

  • Statement III is true. If we substitute $(1,2,3)$ into $f$, we get \[ f(1,2,3) = \ln(1\cdot2\cdot(3-1)) = \ln(4), \] and $f_x$ is also defined at $(1,2,3)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} f_x(1,2,3) &=\dfrac 11 = 1. \end{align*}

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'.

example.title: Identifying Points Where Partial Derivatives Exist

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)?$

  1. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(\sqrt{3},1)$
  2. $f_x(1,\sqrt{3})$ is defined
  3. $f_y(0,1)$ is defined
question.explanation:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_x(x,y) & = \dfrac {\partial} {\partial x} \arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)^2+1} \cdot \dfrac {\partial} {\partial x} \left( \dfrac{x}{y} \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{x^2}{y^2}+1} \cdot \dfrac{1}{y} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{y^2}{x^2+y^2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{y} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{y}{x^2+y^2} \\[7pt] f_y(x,y) & = \dfrac {\partial} {\partial y} \arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)^2+1} \cdot \dfrac {\partial} {\partial y} \left( \dfrac{x}{y} \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{x^2}{y^2}+1} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{x}{y^2}\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{y^2}{x^2+y^2} \cdot \left(-\dfrac{x}{y^2}\right) \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2} \end{align*}

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)$, where we have \[ f(\sqrt{3},1)= \arctan\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}, \] and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(\sqrt{3},1)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} f_x(\sqrt{3},1) &= \dfrac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^2+1^2} = \dfrac{1}{4} \\[5pt] f_y(\sqrt{3},1) &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{3})^2+1^2} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \end{align*}

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})$, where we have \[ f(1,\sqrt{3})=\arctan\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)=\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \] and $f_x$ is also defined at $(1,\sqrt{3})\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} f_x(1,\sqrt{3}) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1^2+(\sqrt{3})^2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}. \end{align*}

  • Statement III is also true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have \[ f(0,1)=\arctan\left(\dfrac{0}{1}\right)=0, \] and $f_y$ is also defined at $(0,1)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} f_y(0,1) = -\dfrac{0}{0^2+1^2} =0. \end{align*}

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\ln\left({x-y} \right)?$

  1. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(0,-1)$
  2. $f_x(0,1)$ is defined
  3. $f_y(1,1)$ is defined
question.explanation:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_x(x,y) & = \dfrac {\partial} {\partial x} \left( \ln\left({x-y} \right) \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{x-y}\cdot 1\\[5pt] & =\dfrac{1}{x-y} \\[7pt] f_y(x,y) & = \dfrac {\partial} {\partial x} \left( \ln\left({x-y} \right) \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{x-y}\cdot (-1)\\[5pt] & =-\dfrac{1}{x-y} \end{align*}

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,-1)$, where we have \[ f(0,-1)=\ln\left({0-(-1)} \right)=\ln\left(1\right)=0, \] and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(0,-1)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} f_x(0,-1) &= \dfrac{1}{0-(-1)} = \dfrac{1}{1}=1 \\[5pt] f_y(0,-1) &= -\dfrac{1}{0-(-1)} = -\dfrac{1}{1}=-1 \end{align*}

  • Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into $f$, we get \[ f(0,1) =\ln(0-1)= \ln(-1), \] which is undefined. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

  • Statement III is false. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into $f$, we get \[ f(1,1)=\ln(1-1)= \ln(0) . \]which is also undefined. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y,z)=\dfrac{z^2}{x^2 - y^2}?$

  1. The partial derivative with respect to $x$ is defined at $(1,-1,0)$
  2. $f_x(0,1,1)$ is defined
  3. $f_z(1,1,0)$ is defined
question.explanation:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= -\dfrac{z^2}{(x^2 - y^2)^2} \cdot (2x) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{2xz^2}{(x^2 - y^2)^2} \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= -\dfrac{z^2}{(x^2 - y^2)^2} \cdot (-2y) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2yz^2}{(x^2 - y^2)^2} \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}&=\dfrac{2z}{x^2 - y^2} \end{align*}

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

  • Statement I is false. If we substitute $(1,-1,0)$ into $f$, we get \[ f(1,-1,0) = \dfrac{(0)^2}{(1)^2+(-1)^2} = \dfrac{0}{0}, \] which is undefined since we have division by zero. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(0,1,1)$, where we have \[ f(0,1,1)=\dfrac{(1)^2}{(0)^2-(1)^2}=-1, \] and $f_x$ is also defined at $(0,1,1)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} f_x(0,1,1) &= -\dfrac{2(0)(1)}{(0)^2-(1)^2} = 0. \end{align*}

  • Statement III is false. If we substitute $(1,1,0)$ into $f$, we get \[ f(1,1,0) = \dfrac{(0)^2}{(1)^2-(1)^2} = \dfrac{0}{0}, \] which is undefined since we have division by zero. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II only'.

example.title: Identifying Points Where Partial Derivatives Exist

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac xy?$

  1. Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(2,-1)$
  2. $f_x(1,0)$ is defined
  3. $f_y(0,1)$ is defined
question.explanation:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} f_x(x,y) & = \dfrac {\partial} {\partial x} \left( \dfrac xy \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac 1y\\[7pt] f_y(x,y) & = \dfrac {\partial} {\partial y} \left(\dfrac xy \right) \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{x}{y^2} \end{align*}

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(2,-1)$, where we have \[ f(2,-1)=\dfrac 2{(-1)}=-2, \] and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(2,-1)\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} f_x(2,-1) &= \dfrac{1}{-1} = -1 \\[5pt] f_y(2,-1) &= -\dfrac{2}{(-1)^2} = -2 \end{align*}

  • Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into $f$, we get \[ f(1,0) =\dfrac10 \] which is undefined since we have division by zero. Since the function is not defined at the point, the derivative is also undefined.

  • Statement III is true. If we substitute $(0,1)$ into $f$, we get \[ f(0,1)=\dfrac 01 =0, \] and $f_y$ is also defined at $(0,1)\mathbin{:}$ \[f_y(0,1) = \dfrac{-0}{1^2}=0\]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".
